learning.title: Learning Panel
learning.stateNear: Closer stars have a larger parallax angle and appear to shift more.
learning.stateFar: Distant stars have a parallax angle too small to detect any movement.
learning.stateOverhead: In the overhead view, you can see how the line of sight to a nearby star shifts as Earth orbits the Sun.
learning.stateObserver: In observer view, nearby stars appear to shift periodically against the background of distant stars.
learning.hint1: Move the distance slider to explore the relationship between distance and parallax angle.
learning.hint2: Press play to watch the star's position change over one year.
learning.hint3: Use 'Jan/Jul Comparison' mode to see the maximum shift over half a year.
learning.parsecDef: 1 parsec (pc) = the distance at which parallax angle equals 1 arcsecond. ≈ 3.26 light-years.
learning.parallaxFormula: Relationship between parallax p [arcsec] and distance d [pc]: d = 1/p

dist-from-parallax.question: What is the distance of a star with a parallax angle of {{p}} arcseconds?

which-is-closer.question: Star A has parallax {{p1}}″ and Star B has parallax {{p2}}″. Which is closer?
which-is-closer.explanation: A larger parallax means a closer star. {{closer}} is closer, at {{d}} pc.

parsec-def.question: Which correctly defines 1 parsec?
choices: Distance at which parallax = 1 arcsecond (≈ 3.26 ly)
Distance light travels in one year (1 light-year)
parsec-def.explanation: One parsec is the distance at which annual parallax equals 1 arcsecond, equivalent to about 3.26 light-years (≈ 206,265 AU).

aberration.label: Annual Aberration
aberration.explain: Apparent shift caused by Earth's orbital velocity (~30 km/s) vs the speed of light (v/c ≈ 1/10000). Independent of star distance.
aberration.phaseNote: In this model all stars lie in the equatorial plane, so aberration produces a 1D back-and-forth shift in RA only. In the real sky the path is elliptical (circular near the ecliptic poles), depending on the star's ecliptic latitude.
